explanations.answer: Is seventy men ruling better than one
explanations.explanation: Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal, wants his uncles to ask whether it's better to have seventy men rule, all of Jerubbaal's sons, or just one man. Then he adds, "Remember that I am your own flesh and blood." I think he's tilting the question toward himself before anybody answers. Friend, that's a pitch with the answer already baked in.

explanations.answer: Is Baal better than the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's not the question Abimelech sends. He asks whether seventy men ruling is better than one man. Baal-berith does show up in this story, though, since the silver comes from its temple a few verses later. The question itself is all about who rules.

explanations.answer: Is peace better than fighting Midian
explanations.explanation: Midian isn't in Abimelech's question. He asks whether it's better to have seventy men rule or just one. Midian comes up later, when Jotham, Abimelech's youngest brother, says their father delivered Shechem from the hand of Midian. For now, the question is about how many rulers.

The text says the leaders of Shechem were inclined to follow Abimelech because "He is our brother." That's the reason they give. Not his record, not his wisdom. I think a family tie can feel like plenty when someone's selling it hard.
The leaders never say that. The reason they give is "He is our brother." The text doesn't call Abimelech the oldest, and it doesn't make birth order their reason. Their reason is family.

Abimelech isn't the one credited with that. Jotham later says his father fought for Shechem and risked his life to deliver them from the hand of Midian. The reason the leaders give for following Abimelech is "He is our brother."

That's it. The seventy shekels of silver come from the temple of Baal-berith, a false god. The silver for this plan comes straight out of a temple, and I think that tells you where Shechem's heart is sitting. Hold on to that detail, friend.

Dagon is a real name in the Bible, but it's not the one here. Dagon is the god in the temple in Ashdod, where the Philistines took the ark of God (1 Samuel 5:1-2). In this story, the silver comes from the temple of Baal-berith.

Rimmon has a temple in the Bible too, but not in this story. Naaman, commander of Aram's army, mentions the temple of Rimmon (2 Kings 5:18). The silver Abimelech gets comes from the temple of Baal-berith.

True. Abimelech hired some "worthless and reckless men to follow him." That's what the seventy shekels buy: a crew. I think when a man has to pay for his followers, that tells you something about his leadership.
Actually, it's true. The text says Abimelech took the silver and hired some "worthless and reckless men to follow him." The silver bought him followers. Nobody just showed up for free.

Yes. Jotham survived because he hid himself. The text gives that reason and no other. Being the youngest and staying out of sight is how he got through the day, and I think he had a lot to carry after it.

explanations.answer: He was out in the fields
explanations.explanation: The text never says Jotham was in the fields. It says he survived because he hid himself. That's the reason it gives. It doesn't tell us where he was hiding.

The text doesn't say that. It says Abimelech went to his father's house in Ophrah, and that Jotham survived because he hid himself. So hiding is the reason, and the text doesn't put him in Shechem. Shechem comes into his story later, when he speaks to its leaders.

King. The leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered beside the oak at the pillar and proceeded to make Abimelech their king. That's the word the text uses. It's a big title for a man whose crew was hired with silver from a temple.
The text doesn't say judge here. It says the leaders proceeded to make Abimelech their king. That's the title they give him.
No priest in this verse. The leaders gather beside the oak at the pillar and make Abimelech their king. The text names a throne, not a temple job.

Yes, Jotham climbs to the top of Mount Gerizim, raises his voice and cries out. Nobody has to wonder whether he can be heard up there. I think a man who hid from his brothers' killer has decided he's done staying quiet, and he picks a spot to be heard.
Mount Carmel is a real mountain in the Bible, but it's not this one. Elijah, the prophet, called Israel to Mount Carmel in his day (1 Kings 18:20). Jotham goes to the top of Mount Gerizim.
Mount Tabor shows up elsewhere in Judges. Barak, Israel's commander under Deborah, gathered his men there (Judges 4:6, 12). Jotham's mountain is Gerizim.

explanations.answer: It won't stop giving its oil to rule
explanations.explanation: The olive tree says, "Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?" Its answer is a question, and the question shows it won't give up its oil. The olive tree already has a job it likes. I think it'd rather keep making oil than sit on a throne.

explanations.answer: It will rule if all trees obey it
explanations.explanation: That's not what the olive tree says. It never sets a condition. It asks whether it should stop giving its oil that honors both God and man to hold sway over the trees.

explanations.answer: It needs time to think it over
explanations.explanation: The olive tree doesn't ask for time. It asks, "Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?" That question is its answer. It's staying with its oil.

The fig tree turns the job down. It says, "Should I stop giving my sweetness and my good fruit, to hold sway over the trees?" So the trees have been told no twice. Two trees down, and nobody's volunteering.

False. The fig tree asks, "Should I stop giving my sweetness and my good fruit, to hold sway over the trees?" It keeps its sweetness and its good fruit and doesn't take the job. Nobody's lining up for this one.
Wine. The grapevine says, "Should I stop giving my wine that cheers both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?" Same pattern as the olive and the fig. The grapevine has its work, and it keeps it.
Oil belongs to the olive tree, the first one the trees ask. The grapevine's gift is wine, the kind that cheers both God and man. Good guess, but it's the wrong tree.
Shade comes up later, and it's the thornbush who talks about it. The grapevine says it won't stop giving its wine that cheers both God and man. So you've got the right story, just the wrong speaker.

The thornbush says, "…come and find refuge in my shade." That's the offer, with an if attached. Friend, I've got a lot of questions about how much shade a thornbush can really give. But that's the offer in the story.
No fruit request from the thornbush. Giving good fruit is what the fig tree talks about when it turns the job down. The thornbush tells the trees to come and find refuge in its shade.
The text doesn't say anything about bowing. The thornbush's offer is, "…come and find refuge in my shade." That's the instruction, and the text doesn't give any other.
Stone. Jotham says the seventy sons were killed on a single stone. I think this one hurts, and it's a heavy part of the story. It's a hard line to hear.
The text doesn't say altar. Jotham says the seventy sons were killed on a single stone. I think this one hurts, and it's heavy. He puts it plainly because it happened.
The word isn't hill. Jotham says his father's seventy sons were killed on a single stone. I think this part hurts, and it's okay to feel that. The text is plain about it.
True. Jotham says they made Abimelech, "the son of his maidservant," king "because he is your brother." That's the same reason the leaders gave back in verse 3. Jotham is holding it up to the light.
It's true. Jotham says the leaders made Abimelech, "the son of his maidservant," king over the leaders of Shechem because he is their brother. Family tie, that's the reason Jotham names.

explanations.answer: Rejoice in Abimelech and he in them
explanations.explanation: Jotham says, "…then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you." That's the good side of his if. It only holds if they've acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his house. The condition is the whole point.

explanations.answer: Have rest in their land again
explanations.explanation: Jotham doesn't say that. If they've acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal's house, he says, "…then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you." Rest in the land is not part of his words.

explanations.answer: Be blessed with a good harvest
explanations.explanation: No harvest in Jotham's words. If they've acted faithfully and honestly, he says, "…then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you." That's the outcome he names.

Fire. Jotham says, "…may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo," and may fire come from the leaders and consume Abimelech. It goes both ways. Fire also showed up in the thornbush's words, so Jotham's story and his message are tied together.
No floods in Jotham's words. He says fire, from Abimelech to the leaders and from the leaders to Abimelech. It goes both directions.
Jotham doesn't mention famine. He says, "…may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo," and the same the other way. Fire is the word.
Beer. Jotham runs away, escaping to Beer, and he lives there. The text doesn't tell us much about the place. It does tell us he got there.
Bethel is a real place in the Bible, but it's not where Jotham goes. Jacob named it Bethel long before this (Genesis 28:19). Jotham escapes to Beer.
Hebron is in the Bible too, but not here. Abraham settled near Hebron in his day (Genesis 13:18). Jotham escapes to Beer.
Yes. The text says Jotham "lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech." He has seen what Abimelech did to his seventy brothers. That fear is the reason the text gives for his staying in Beer.

explanations.answer: He wants to raise an army
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. It says Jotham "lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech." Fear is the only reason it gives.

The text doesn't say that about Beer. It says Jotham lived there "for fear of his brother Abimelech." Abimelech's mother's family was in Shechem. About Jotham's family in Beer, the text gives us nothing.
